content.description: Adai batter doesn't ferment/rise even after the usual resting time.
content.symptoms: The batter looks the same as when first ground, with no bubbles or rise.
content.diagnosis: Batter kept somewhere too cold, or too little lentil content relative to rice to drive fermentation.
fixes: Move the batter somewhere warmer and give it more time
If it still won't ferment, adai can still be made from unfermented batter -- it will be denser but still cook through fine
prevention: Use a good ratio of lentils to rice (adai traditionally uses more lentils than idli/dosa batter) and keep it warm while fermenting

content.description: Appam comes out dense and flat rather than with the characteristic lacy, thin edges.
content.symptoms: No visible lace pattern at the edges; the appam looks closer to a thick pancake.
content.diagnosis: Batter not fermented enough, or not swirled properly in the appachatti while cooking.
fixes: Let the batter ferment longer next time until it's visibly airy
Swirl the appachatti quickly right after pouring the batter so it coats the sides thinly
prevention: Make sure the batter has the right thin, pourable consistency -- too thick won't swirl into a lacy edge

content.description: Idli/dosa batter turns unpleasantly sour from fermenting too long.
content.symptoms: Strong sour smell and taste beyond the normal mild tang.
content.diagnosis: Left to ferment too long or in too warm an environment.
fixes: Use it for dosa (which tolerates more sourness) rather than idli
Add a pinch of baking soda to balance sourness
prevention: Refrigerate the batter once it has fermented enough

content.description: The bottom layer of dum biryani burns or sticks before the dish finishes cooking.
content.symptoms: A scorched, bitter smell and a blackened layer at the very bottom of the pot.
content.diagnosis: Heat too high for the dum stage, or not enough fat/liquid lining the bottom of the pot before layering.
fixes: Lower the heat immediately and, if using a stovetop, place a tawa underneath the pot to diffuse heat more evenly
Scrape off only the burnt layer and serve the rest -- the burnt flavour doesn't usually spread far
prevention: Grease the bottom of the pot well before layering
Use a heavy-bottomed pot and keep the dum heat on the lowest setting possible, or finish in a low oven instead of stovetop

content.description: Biryani comes out as one uniform mass rather than distinct layers of rice and meat/vegetables.
content.symptoms: No visible separation when serving -- everything is mixed together rather than layered.
content.diagnosis: Not enough care taken while layering, or too much mixing/stirring during the dum stage.
fixes: Avoid stirring once layers are assembled -- serve by scooping down through the layers rather than mixing first
prevention: Layer deliberately (rice, then meat/veg, then rice again) and avoid disturbing the layers until it's time to serve

content.description: Meat in biryani remains tough and chewy rather than tender.
content.symptoms: Meat pieces are difficult to bite through even though the rice is cooked.
content.diagnosis: Meat not marinated long enough, or the dum (steaming) stage too short for the cut of meat used.
fixes: If already served, a quick extra steam (adding a splash of water, covering, and cooking on low heat a bit longer) can help soften it somewhat
prevention: Marinate meat longer, especially tougher cuts, and use a yogurt-based marinade which helps tenderize
Match the dum cooking time to the specific cut and type of meat being used

content.description: Biryani rice turns out mushy and clumped rather than separate, fluffy grains.
content.symptoms: Grains stick together and lose their individual shape; the dish looks more like a thick pilaf than layered biryani.
content.diagnosis: Too much water relative to rice, overcooking, or stirring the rice too much after it's added to the pot.
fixes: Use slightly less water than usual next time and avoid stirring once the rice goes in
If already mushy, spread it out on a wide tray to cool and let excess steam escape rather than leaving it covered in the pot
prevention: Rinse rice well before cooking to remove excess surface starch
Use the dum (sealed, low-heat steam) method rather than boiling the rice fully in the pot

content.description: Ground chutney turns watery and separates instead of staying emulsified.
content.symptoms: Liquid pools on top after grinding or sitting.
content.diagnosis: Too much water added while grinding, or chutney sat too long before serving.
fixes: Grind with minimal water and adjust consistency at the end
Serve fresh
prevention: Add water gradually while grinding

content.description: Coconut/vegetable chutney develops an unexpected bitter edge.
content.symptoms: Bitterness noticeable despite normal ingredients.
content.diagnosis: Garlic or spices burnt during tempering, or the brown part of the coconut ground in.
fixes: Redo the tempering carefully at moderate heat
Scrape away the brown coconut skin before grinding
prevention: Temper on medium heat and watch closely
Use only the white coconut flesh

content.description: Coconut chutney develops a pinkish tinge after sitting for a while.
content.symptoms: A faint pink or reddish discolouration appears in white coconut chutney that wasn't there when freshly made.
content.diagnosis: A natural enzymatic reaction in fresh coconut when exposed to air and certain ingredients like tamarind or chilli over time -- not spoilage on its own, but can indicate it's aging.
fixes: It's generally still fine to eat shortly after this appears, but check smell and taste before serving
Make chutney fresh and consume within a day for best colour and taste
prevention: Store coconut chutney covered and refrigerated, and consume promptly rather than keeping it for multiple days

content.description: Lentils/dal remain firm even after extended cooking.
content.symptoms: Dal stays grainy/hard rather than turning creamy.
content.diagnosis: Old dal stock, hard water, or salt/acidic ingredients added too early.
fixes: Continue cooking with more water
Add a pinch of baking soda to help soften (use sparingly)
prevention: Add salt and tamarind/tomato only after the dal is fully cooked soft

content.description: Dosa batter is too thick to spread into a thin, even crepe.
content.symptoms: The batter tears or clumps instead of spreading smoothly across the pan.
content.diagnosis: Not enough water added when grinding or after fermentation.
fixes: Thin the batter with a little water, mixed in gradually until it reaches a pourable, spreadable consistency
prevention: Check consistency before fermenting and adjust water then, since fermentation itself can also thicken the batter slightly

content.description: Dosa batter is too thin and runs off the pan instead of holding a shape.
content.symptoms: The batter spreads unevenly into holes or a very thin, patchy dosa.
content.diagnosis: Too much water added relative to the rice and urad dal.
fixes: Thicken by grinding in a small additional amount of soaked rice or urad dal, or simply let some water evaporate by resting it a while uncovered
prevention: Add water gradually while grinding and check consistency before adding more, rather than adding it all at once

content.description: Dosa turns out soft/chewy instead of thin and crisp.
content.symptoms: Dosa doesn't crisp at the edges even after cooking.
content.diagnosis: Batter too thick, too much rice flour vs. urad dal, or tawa not hot enough.
fixes: Thin the batter slightly with water
Cook on a hotter tawa
Spread the batter thinner
prevention: Get the rice-to-urad-dal ratio right
Preheat the tawa well before pouring batter

content.description: Dosa tears or sticks when trying to flip or remove it from the tawa.
content.symptoms: Batter clings to the pan surface instead of releasing cleanly.
content.diagnosis: Tawa not seasoned/heated properly, or too little oil.
fixes: Heat the tawa properly and season it with oil before the first dosa
Use enough oil around the edges
Let the dosa cook fully before attempting to lift it
prevention: Use a well-seasoned cast-iron or non-stick tawa
Maintain consistent medium heat

content.description: Steam escapes during the dum stage, and the biryani doesn't cook evenly or stay moist.
content.symptoms: Rice near the top stays undercooked while the pot loses visible steam from the lid.
content.diagnosis: The pot lid isn't sealed well enough to trap steam.
fixes: Seal the lid with a simple dough strip (atta) around the rim, or use a tight-fitting heavy lid with a damp cloth underneath it
prevention: Check that the pot and lid fit tightly before starting the dum stage, and seal any gaps before placing on low heat

content.description: South Indian filter coffee tastes bitter/harsh instead of smooth.
content.symptoms: Sharp bitterness overwhelms the coffee-chicory flavour.
content.diagnosis: Over-extraction (too long a drip time or too fine a grind) or too high a coffee-to-water ratio.
fixes: Dilute with more hot milk
Use a coarser grind or reduce drip time next time
prevention: Follow the traditional slow-drip method for the right extraction

content.description: Fish pieces disintegrate into the curry instead of holding their shape.
content.symptoms: Fish turns mushy and loses its distinct pieces when stirred.
content.diagnosis: Fish stirred too much while cooking, or simmered too long/too vigorously.
fixes: Stop stirring once the fish is added -- gently shake or swirl the pan instead of using a spoon
prevention: Add fish pieces near the end of cooking and simmer gently rather than at a hard boil
Choose a firmer fish variety if the curry needs more simmering time

content.description: Stored ghee develops an off, rancid smell/taste.
content.symptoms: Ghee smells sour or 'off' rather than nutty and fresh.
content.diagnosis: Moisture contamination or prolonged exposure to heat/light.
fixes: Discard rancid ghee
prevention: Always use a completely dry spoon
Store in an airtight container away from direct heat/sunlight

content.description: Gongura pachadi tastes unexpectedly bitter rather than pleasantly tangy.
content.symptoms: A sharp bitterness that overwhelms the characteristic sourness of the dish.
content.diagnosis: Gongura leaves cooked too long at high heat, or older/tougher leaves used.
fixes: Balance with a bit more jaggery or oil-tempered spice to offset the bitterness in that batch
prevention: Use young, tender gongura leaves where possible, and avoid prolonged high-heat cooking which can bring out bitterness

content.description: Idiyappam strands clump into a dense mass instead of staying separate and light.
content.symptoms: The steamed noodles stick together in a solid lump rather than falling apart into individual strands.
content.diagnosis: Dough too wet, or strands pressed too close together on the steaming plate.
fixes: Spread the pressed strands out more loosely on the plate before steaming
If the dough feels too soft, add a little more rice flour next time before pressing
prevention: Use water at the right temperature (usually just-boiled, mixed in quickly) when making the dough -- too much water makes it stick

content.description: Idli/dosa batter fails to rise after the usual fermentation period.
content.symptoms: Batter stays flat and smells the same as when mixed; no bubbles.
content.diagnosis: Ambient temperature too cold, too little urad dal, or old/dead fermenting culture (no starter batter).
fixes: Keep the batter in a warm spot (oven with light on, or near a warm appliance)
Increase the urad dal proportion slightly
Add a spoon of old fermented batter as a starter
prevention: Ferment in a warm season/location
Use fresh urad dal
Don't over-wash away the natural yeasts

content.description: After a full night the idli/dosa batter has not risen - it is the same volume, flat on top, with no bubbles or sour smell - and the idlis come out dense and hard.
content.symptoms: No rise; no domed surface; smells raw, not sour; heavy rubbery idli.
content.diagnosis: The batter was kept too cold, or not left long enough, or the salt was added in a large amount before fermenting, or the urad dal was old / poorly ground.
fixes: Move the batter somewhere warmer (near the stove, in the oven with just the light on, or wrapped in a towel) and give it several more hours.
Stir in a spoon of live batter or plain yoghurt as a starter and wait again.
If it still will not rise, add a pinch of baking soda just before steaming for that batch and grind a fresh batch of urad dal next time.
prevention: Ferment at 25-30 C; in a cold kitchen use the oven light or an instant-pot yoghurt setting.
Add most of the salt after fermentation, not before.
Use fresh urad dal and grind it light and fluffy; add a few fenugreek seeds when soaking.

root_causes: old or badly ground urad dal

content.description: The steaming water runs low or boils dry partway through steaming idlis.
content.symptoms: Idlis near the end of steaming look uncooked or a burning smell starts from the pot.
content.diagnosis: Not enough water added at the start for the expected steaming duration.
fixes: If caught in time, carefully add more hot water to the pot without disturbing the idli stand, and continue steaming
prevention: Fill the steaming vessel with enough water for the full expected steaming time before starting, checking the level if steaming a large batch

content.description: Steamed idlis come out dense and hard instead of soft and spongy.
content.symptoms: Idli is compact, doesn't spring back when pressed.
content.diagnosis: Under-fermented batter, batter ground too coarse, or over-steaming.
fixes: Steam for the correct time only (usually 8-12 minutes)
Ensure batter is well-fermented and light before steaming
prevention: Grind batter to the right smooth-but-slightly-grainy consistency
Don't skip fermentation time

content.description: Kesari (rava sheera/halwa) has hard, undissolved lumps of rava instead of a smooth texture.
content.symptoms: Gritty or hard bits scattered through an otherwise soft dish.
content.diagnosis: Rava added to hot water/liquid too quickly without stirring continuously, or not roasted first.
fixes: Pass it through a sieve to remove the worst lumps, or continue cooking with extra liquid while stirring vigorously to break them down
prevention: Roast the rava in ghee first until fragrant, then add the hot liquid gradually while stirring continuously, not all at once

content.description: Murukku cracks or breaks apart as soon as it hits the hot oil.
content.symptoms: Pieces fall apart into fragments rather than frying as one intact spiral.
content.diagnosis: Dough too dry/crumbly, or not kneaded enough before pressing.
fixes: Knead the dough a little longer with slightly more water or oil until it holds together smoothly before pressing
prevention: Rest the dough briefly, covered, before pressing so it stays pliable
Press directly into the hot oil rather than letting shaped pieces sit and dry out first

content.description: Murukku turns out hard and tough to bite rather than crisp and light.
content.symptoms: Dense, difficult to bite through even though it looks properly fried.
content.diagnosis: Too much rice flour relative to urad dal flour, or oil not hot enough so it fried too slowly.
fixes: Adjust the flour ratio next time toward a bit more urad dal flour for a lighter texture
Fry in properly hot oil so the murukku cooks through quickly rather than slowly hardening
prevention: Test oil temperature with a small piece of dough first -- it should sizzle and rise promptly

content.description: Papad doesn't puff up fully when fried or roasted.
content.symptoms: Papad stays flat or only partially expands.
content.diagnosis: Oil not hot enough (if frying) or papad too old/dried out.
fixes: Increase oil temperature and fry briefly
Use fresher papad
prevention: Store papad in an airtight container away from moisture

content.description: Stored papads stick together and tear when trying to separate them.
content.symptoms: Papads clump into a stack that won't pull apart cleanly.
content.diagnosis: Humidity getting into the storage container, softening the papads.
fixes: Separate them carefully while still slightly pliable rather than fully dried and brittle
prevention: Store in an airtight container with a moisture absorber if the climate is humid, and keep them fully dried before stacking

content.description: Milk-based payasam curdles/splits instead of staying smooth.
content.symptoms: Visible curdled specks in the payasam.
content.diagnosis: Adding an acidic ingredient (like fruit) to hot milk too quickly, or milk cooked at too high heat for too long.
fixes: Add acidic ingredients off the heat and gradually
Cook milk-based payasam on low-medium heat
prevention: Temper acidic additions in slowly at the end

content.description: Payasam has lumps rather than a smooth, even consistency.
content.symptoms: Small clumps of rice, jaggery, or coconut milk solids visible or felt while eating.
content.diagnosis: Jaggery not fully dissolved/strained, or the base ingredient not cooked down fully before adding milk.
fixes: Strain the jaggery syrup before adding it to remove any undissolved bits or impurities
Mash or blend lightly if lumps are from undercooked rice/dal
prevention: Always dissolve jaggery in a little hot water and strain it before adding to the payasam

content.description: Payasam thickens into something closer to a pudding than a pourable, spoonable payasam.
content.symptoms: The payasam sets firm or very dense as it cools, losing its characteristic flowing consistency.
content.diagnosis: Too much reduction of the milk, or too much of the starchy base ingredient (rice, vermicelli, etc.) relative to liquid.
fixes: Loosen it by warming through with a little extra milk, stirred in gradually until it reaches the right consistency
prevention: Remember that payasam continues to thicken as it cools, so take it off the heat slightly thinner than the final texture you want

content.description: Pesarattu tears or sticks to the pan when trying to flip or remove it.
content.symptoms: The batter won't release cleanly, tearing into pieces rather than lifting off whole.
content.diagnosis: Pan not hot enough or not seasoned/oiled enough, or batter spread too thick.
fixes: Make sure the pan is properly hot before pouring, and use a thin, even layer of oil around the edges
Spread the batter a bit thinner next time
prevention: Season a cast-iron or non-stick pan well and let it heat fully before the first pesarattu

content.description: Pickle develops mould during storage.
content.symptoms: Visible fuzzy growth on the surface or jar sides.
content.diagnosis: Insufficient oil/salt as a preservative, moisture contamination, or a non-dry serving spoon used.
fixes: Discard affected pickle
Remake with adequate oil/salt and ensure the jar and spoon are completely dry
prevention: Always use a dry spoon
Keep pickle submerged in oil
Store in a cool, dry place

content.description: Oil in a pickle separates and floats visibly rather than staying incorporated.
content.symptoms: A distinct oil layer on top of the jar that doesn't recombine when stirred.
content.diagnosis: Normal for oil-based pickles over time, but excessive separation usually means too much oil was used relative to the solid content.
fixes: Simply stir or shake before serving -- this is largely cosmetic unless the proportions were badly off
prevention: Use oil in the proportion traditional for that specific pickle recipe rather than adding extra 'for safety'

content.description: Pickle tastes overwhelmingly salty rather than balanced.
content.symptoms: Salt dominates over the sour/spicy notes of the pickle.
content.diagnosis: Too much salt added relative to the amount of main ingredient, often from over-correcting for preservation.
fixes: Mix in some unsalted, freshly prepared portion of the same vegetable/fruit to dilute the overall salt level, if practical
Serve smaller portions alongside other dishes to balance the saltiness in the overall meal
prevention: Measure salt carefully rather than adding by feel, especially for pickles meant for long storage where it's tempting to over-salt

labels: Pongal came out dry and stiff

content.description: The finished pongal is thick, stiff and sliceable instead of soft and creamy, and it firms up further as it cools.
content.symptoms: Holds sharp edges; hard to stir; pasty rather than creamy on the tongue.
content.diagnosis: Not enough cooking liquid, or the mixture was cooked/held too long after the water was absorbed.
fixes: Stir in hot water a little at a time over low heat until it loosens to a soft dropping consistency, then fold in a spoon of extra ghee.
Serve immediately; pongal always thickens on standing.
prevention: Use about 4.5-5 cups water per 1 cup rice-plus-dal.
Take it off the heat while it still looks slightly loose.

root_causes: fast pressure release drying the surface

content.description: Vegetables in poriyal remain hard/raw in the centre despite looking cooked on the outside.
content.symptoms: A raw, starchy bite in the middle of the vegetable pieces.
content.diagnosis: Pieces cut too large, or cooked too briefly/on too high heat so the outside cooked faster than the inside.
fixes: Cover and cook a little longer on lower heat to let the heat penetrate through before finishing uncovered to dry it out
prevention: Cut vegetables into smaller, even pieces so they cook through more quickly and evenly

content.description: Poriyal turns out watery and soupy instead of dry and lightly coated with coconut.
content.symptoms: Liquid pools at the bottom of the pan instead of the vegetables staying dry and separate.
content.diagnosis: Vegetables released too much water during cooking, often from cooking covered for too long or adding water unnecessarily.
fixes: Cook uncovered on higher heat for the last few minutes to let excess moisture evaporate
prevention: Avoid adding extra water -- most vegetables release enough of their own moisture to cook through
Cut vegetables evenly so they cook at the same rate without needing extra liquid

content.description: Puttu turns out dry and falls apart instead of holding together lightly.
content.symptoms: Puttu crumbles excessively when unmoulded.
content.diagnosis: Rice flour not moistened enough before steaming.
fixes: Sprinkle and mix water into the flour until it just holds together when pressed, before steaming
prevention: Test the flour's moisture with a pinch-test before layering into the steamer

content.description: Puttu turns out soggy/gummy instead of light and fluffy.
content.symptoms: Puttu feels dense and sticky.
content.diagnosis: Too much water added to the rice flour before steaming.
fixes: Reduce the water slightly next time and steam a touch longer
prevention: Add water gradually, testing texture as you go

content.description: Rasam lacks the light frothy top that indicates it's properly finished.
content.symptoms: Rasam looks flat/thin on top instead of slightly frothy.
content.diagnosis: Boiled too vigorously for too long, or rasam powder added too early and cooked out.
fixes: Heat gently and remove from heat as soon as it just starts to froth, don't let it hard-boil
prevention: Add rasam powder near the end and avoid a rolling boil after

content.description: Rasam tastes overpoweringly sour rather than balanced.
content.symptoms: Sourness dominates over the pepper/tomato/spice notes.
content.diagnosis: Too much tamarind or tomato relative to water and spice.
fixes: Dilute with more water/dal water
Balance with a touch of jaggery
prevention: Measure tamarind extract carefully

content.description: Rasam tastes watery and lacks body, even though the flavour seasoning is right.
content.symptoms: Thin, almost like flavoured water, missing the usual light-but-rounded mouthfeel.
content.diagnosis: Not enough dal water/stock used as the base, or dal cooked separately and not incorporated.
fixes: Add a little mashed cooked dal or dal cooking water to give it body
prevention: Always use the water dal was cooked in as part of the rasam base rather than plain water

content.description: Cooked rice turns out sticky/mushy instead of separate grains.
content.symptoms: Grains clump together and lose shape.
content.diagnosis: Too much water or overcooked.
fixes: Use the correct water-to-rice ratio for the variety
Reduce cooking time slightly
prevention: Rinse rice before cooking to remove excess surface starch

content.description: Rice grains remain hard/uncooked in the centre.
content.symptoms: Bite resistance is too firm, grains taste starchy-raw.
content.diagnosis: Too little water or insufficient cooking time.
fixes: Add a little more water and continue cooking covered
Extend cooking time
prevention: Measure water correctly for the rice variety used

content.description: Sambar lacks the expected tangy, spiced depth of flavour.
content.symptoms: Tastes flat despite having the right ingredients.
content.diagnosis: Too little tamarind/sambar powder, or tempering (tadka) skipped or added too early.
fixes: Adjust tamarind and sambar powder to taste
Add a fresh tempering of mustard seeds, curry leaves, and asafoetida just before serving
prevention: Always finish with a fresh, hot tempering

content.description: Sambar podi (spice powder) tastes bitter and burnt rather than toasty and aromatic.
content.symptoms: A sharp, acrid smell and bitter aftertaste in the finished powder.
content.diagnosis: Spices roasted on too high heat or for too long before grinding.
fixes: If only lightly over-roasted, use a smaller quantity in cooking to dilute the bitterness; if badly burnt, it's best to re-roast a fresh batch
prevention: Dry-roast each spice on low to medium heat, stirring constantly, and remove from heat the moment it turns fragrant -- don't wait for visible colour change

content.description: Sambar turns out thin and soup-like instead of a thick stew consistency.
content.symptoms: Sambar doesn't coat the back of a spoon.
content.diagnosis: Too much water added, or dal under-cooked/under-mashed.
fixes: Simmer uncovered to reduce and thicken
Mash the cooked dal well before adding vegetables
prevention: Measure water against dal quantity carefully

content.description: Ground spice powder (sambar podi, rasam podi, etc.) clumps into hard lumps during storage.
content.symptoms: The powder forms solid chunks instead of staying loose and free-flowing.
content.diagnosis: Moisture getting into the container, often from a damp spoon or humid storage conditions.
fixes: Break up the clumps by hand or with a dry spoon before use
Dry-roast the powder briefly in a pan on low heat to drive off moisture, then cool completely before re-storing
prevention: Always use a completely dry spoon, and store in an airtight container away from steam (not right next to the stove)

content.description: Ground spice powder (sambar/rasam podi etc.) loses its fragrance and potency over time.
content.symptoms: Powder smells and tastes flat compared to when freshly made.
content.diagnosis: Prolonged storage, exposure to air/light/moisture, or storing whole roasted spices ground too far in advance.
fixes: Use within a few weeks of grinding for best flavour
prevention: Store in an airtight container away from light and heat
Grind in smaller batches more frequently

content.description: Tamarind extract comes out too thick and pulpy instead of a smooth, pourable liquid.
content.symptoms: Fibrous bits and a paste-like consistency rather than a strained liquid.
content.diagnosis: Not strained well enough, or too little water used when soaking/mashing.
fixes: Add a little more water and strain again through a fine sieve, pressing the pulp to extract remaining liquid
prevention: Soak tamarind in enough warm water and strain thoroughly, discarding the fibrous solids rather than including them

content.description: Tempering (tadka) burns instead of sizzling and releasing aroma.
content.symptoms: Mustard seeds/curry leaves turn black and smell acrid rather than fragrant.
content.diagnosis: Oil too hot or tempering left in the pan too long.
fixes: Discard the burnt tempering and redo it at a slightly lower heat
prevention: Add ingredients to the tempering in the right order (mustard seeds first, curry leaves/asafoetida last) and keep heat moderate

content.description: Vadas turn out greasy/oily instead of crisp and light.
content.symptoms: Vada feels heavy and oil-soaked when bitten.
content.diagnosis: Oil not hot enough when frying, or batter too soft/wet.
fixes: Fry at the correct hot oil temperature (test with a small drop of batter)
Firm up the batter before shaping
prevention: Always test oil temperature before frying a full batch

content.description: Vada turns out dense/flat instead of having the characteristic airy holes.
content.symptoms: Vada lacks the light doughnut-like texture.
content.diagnosis: Batter over- or under-beaten, or not aerated enough before frying.
fixes: Beat the batter well to incorporate air before shaping
prevention: Beat until the batter feels light and slightly increases in volume

content.description: Vatha kuzhambu turns out swimming in oil rather than a balanced, tangy gravy.
content.symptoms: A visible oily layer on top that doesn't incorporate into the gravy.
content.diagnosis: Too much oil used in tempering/cooking relative to the gravy base.
fixes: Skim off the excess oil from the top before serving
Reduce the oil quantity next time, especially in the initial tempering step
prevention: Use oil mainly for tempering the spices, not as a cooking medium for the whole gravy

content.description: Ven pongal turns out runny and soupy instead of soft but holding together.
content.symptoms: The dish pools liquid and doesn't hold its shape on a plate.
content.diagnosis: Too much water relative to rice and dal, or not cooked down enough at the end.
fixes: Continue cooking uncovered, stirring occasionally, until the excess water evaporates and it thickens to the right consistency
prevention: Use the standard ratio (roughly 1 part dal to 4-5 parts rice, with water about 4-5 times the combined grain) and adjust gradually rather than adding all the water upfront
